story_text.value:
Hello, my name is Danny and I created dbhealth to monitor postgres. I have an SRE background and was working in data eng for a couple years.

dbhealth provides verdicts on health and exposes these through: - statsd - prometheus - OTLP - Turbostats (the protocol that powers https://control.turbolytics.io/)

dbhealth also provides table freshness by profiling the most recent row available.

Happy to answer any questions. Thank you!

story_text.value:
Every (personal) agent (like Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, Poke) asks you to connect your email, calendar, and tools again. Permissions are intransparent and every provider ends up building the same integrations.

We think there needs to be an independent tool that holds all connections to third party companies.

That way you can keep auth separate, audit what an agent does, set fine-grained permissions and easily switch between the agent apps.

I built this over the last few days with my friend Konsti. It's open source and we’ve put a lot of care into the self-hosting experience.

Now my Instinct has the same tools as Claude Code and Codex on my laptop.

What are your thoughts about this and how are you handling this today?

story_text.value:
I wanted upcoming events in my calendar, but not entire schedules full of things I don’t follow. So I built PickyCal.

Pick an event source, filter it, and subscribe through CalDAV or an ICS link. For example: Starship launches, the next James Bond cinema release, Classic Tetris World Championship finals. Filters support &, |, !, and parentheses.

PickyCal regularly checks for new events and schedule changes, your calendar picks them up when it syncs. You can try the filters on the website without an account.

I’d love to hear which sources you’d find useful and any suggestions for improvements.

story_text.value:
Back when I lived in Central Florida, it took me years to learn what native plants could benefit wildlife and the local ecosystem as I slowly replaced parts of my yard to make it more resilient to drought. After moving to Seattle a few years ago, I had to start all of that from scratch. LLMs made the process a bit easier but I still had to routinely ask the same kinds of questions over and over, despite being far more familiar with native plants these days and leaning more on native plant societies and botany resources like Doug Tallamy and Joey Santore whose excellent Crime Pays But Botany Doesn't site was recently posted here[1].

A good friend was visiting from Orlando over the summer and told me she was struggling to decide what to plant in her own yard despite her landlord being ok with it. That was enough of an excuse for me to kick off work on Indigene, which is aimed at giving folks just-in-time knowledge about what to plant based on their locale, sun exposure, soil conditions, and their own ecosystem support goals.

Candidly, as many of us have, I've also leaned heavily on LLMs (mostly Claude here) to bring this to life. Largely to avoid saying demonstrably false things, which might be an absurd statement. You can find the GitHub repository[2] a wild array of open data sources I've dug out and cross-referenced to ensure mistakes and hallucinations are unlikely to survive for long. But given today's Indigenous Peoples Day I figured it was past time I shared the projects and invited more scrutiny.

Being the Keep a Changelog guy, you can bet it has extensive release notes[3] generated from the project changelog. Those are also parsed into feature-specific guides so each also lists relevant recent updates.

Lastly, I put together a post[5] that goes into a bit more detail on the story of the project and what I've learned along the way.

I really, really hope people here (and beyond) find it as useful and enlightening as I do.

PS: before it comes up, all the LLM usage for the project is documented[6] and used as warning system in every PR but I think there's a lot more I can do to further reduce it

[1]: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49192566

[2]: https://github.com/olivierlacan/indigene

[3]: https://indigene.app/release-notes/

[4]: https://indigene.app/guide/

[5]: https://constantvariable.net/blog/2026/indigene-native-plant...

[6]: https://indigene.app/llm/

story_text.value:
Hey HN, im Marc, co-founder of ObsessionDB. We are open sourcing ChKit, our tooling to manage schemas, migrations and backfills for clickhouse.

I am a big fan of the type safety drizzle provides for the database. Manage the schema in typescript and generate migrations from it is a powerful workflow. I always wished something like it would exist for clickhouse, so we could manage our analytical workloads the same way. It didn't exist, so we build it.

We build it after running ClickHouse at petabyte scale in our previous company, were we managed hundreds of tables, MVs and endpoints reading from them.

The way it works:

1. You define your schema in typescript, with typed helpers for tables, mv, column types etc.. 2. You generate the migration, that contains the DDL, to get your clickhouse instance from status quo to what your current typescript schema defines 3. Your CI can check for drift 4. You run the generated migration against production 5. You use the defined types in your code, to ingest your data while making sure it has the correct type. Bonus: if your schema change was BC breaking, we generate the sequence on how to backfill the data, into the intermediate table to migrate (this is quite the hard problem with large tables and schema evolution)

In case you have already a clickhouse instance with a schema, you can pull it down and start using ChKit from where you are.

Run our generator to setup the boilerplate:

  npm create chkit@latest
If you folks are running clickhouse in production, I am curious to hear what other challenges you are running into.

title.value: Show HN: Chkit – Schema, migrations and backfills for ClickHouse (like Drizzle)

story_text.value:
I recently had an issue with my right hand, and couldn't use it very effectively. So I was trying to figure out how I could still get work done without typing everything with my right hand.

I looked around for some tools, but then thought, why not try building something myself? The idea was to make an accessibility and productivity tool that lets me get thoughts out of my head and turn them into something useful with less manual effort.

That's how I started building Lucid. You can turn rough input into structured notes, diagrams, and tables, and edit everything afterwards. I'm also using a local AI model through LM Studio.

One use case I had in mind was system design. Imagine thinking through a system, talking about its components, and getting a diagram out of it instead of manually creating everything. I'm currently using a separate dictation app for voice input, so there's still a lot I can improve here.

It started as a way to help myself, but I thought it was a cool thing to build and might be useful to others as well. So sharing it here!

Demo: https://youtu.be/AwlJ8LJbfw4

GitHub: https://github.com/triggeredcode/lucid

Website: https://triggeredcode.github.io/lucid/

title.value: Show HN: Turn spoken thoughts into system design diagrams

story_text.value:
Good evening folks, I built Github merge gate which that checks whether developers understand their own code when they create a PR.

I kept getting sent PRs to review where it was obvious the author had pasted the ticket into an LLM and called it a day.

It's self-hosted (so you can use it in your enterprise environments or privately)

It is BYOK (Anthropic) obviously.

I have two demos in the pull requests here: https://github.com/bhurghundii/vibecheck.dev/pulls - you can see what Vibecheck does (it blocks a PR for clearly showing no attempt vs a PR which gets it right)

I would love feedback, especially from anyone dealing with a similar problem. I do use it for my own projects a lot so expect improvements.

story_text.value:
Hi everyone. Today I’m here to introduce "Ever". a language aiming to be something like a modern-day Turbo C. It features high-level syntax but operates at a low level, designed to run on modern systems.

By the way, don't download the release. That release is from three months ago—back when I created the previous thread—and work on the new version isn't finished yet, so I haven't released it. I started this thread to get your opinions and feedback on the new version.

I can no longer say that the entire language is written in D, because I’ve written the libraries and the Windows interpreter in various languages. However, I can still say that the core of the project is largely written in D.

Ever is made possible thanks to the D community. arsd.simpledisplay and arsd.minigui provides high-level graphics functions, making it easy to create graphical applications. I'm also working on integrating Raylib with Ever to make game development possible.

And to test and build the language, simply run the following command. curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/evrlang/ever/main/install.... | bash

Or clone the repo and run compile.sh.

I sincerely apologize that the documentation isn't finished yet and I haven't had time to add more examples. However, if you have any questions, feel free to reach out to me here so I can help you.

Github link: https://github.com/evrlang/ever Website: https://evrlang.github.io/ever A very special thank you to everyone who gave me technical advice on the previous thread and prompted me to reconsider the language syntax.

title.value: Show HN: Ever – A High-Level Language for Low-Level Purposes

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I'm a big fan of the liquid-dsp C library and thought it'd be fun to bring it over to Rust. I'm calling this library Yagi DSP. liquid-dsp has more than 1300 tests and yagi now has ported and passes more than 95% of them. I've just finished a major refactoring of the library with lots of API churn now behind me and I think it's now ready for external users.

I've still got a lot more I'm hoping to do with it including a streaming graph/dataflow library that I'm building on top of yagi. My goal with that is to create something that's easily embeddable in applications.

The browser demo linked in the README is just a very basic example to show how different modems work in the presence of noise, but it really does use yagi via wasm-bindgen. I think it's a fun 5 minute diversion if you've heard terms like QPSK or QAM but aren't sure what they mean.

You can try out the demo here

https://brian-armstrong.github.io/yagi/lab.html

title.value: Show HN: Yagi, Rust DSP Library
